fields.label: In your own words, what two jobs does the asteroid task ask you to do?
The current position, 1.2 × 10⁸ km, tells us _____.
The velocity, 8,500 m/s at 15°, tells us _____.
Why is a constant-velocity model reasonable here?
Name the five things you need to produce for the transfer task.
Convert 1.2 × 10⁸ km to meters. Show your conversion and units.
Because velocity is in m/s, time must be in _____.
Using 182.5 days for six months, calculate the time in seconds. Show your work.
Toward-Earth component: v × _____ θ.
Sideways component: v × _____ θ.
Calculate both components of 8,500 m/s at 15°. Include units and explain which component changes the toward-Earth position.
Write the position equation, define its symbols, and explain the sign of the toward-Earth velocity.
Use your converted starting position, toward-Earth velocity, and six-month time to predict x_f. Show the calculation with units.
Uncertainty describes _____, rather than a mistake.
For 900 ± 30 m, the lowest value is _____ m and the highest is _____ m.
Explain what ± means to someone who has never studied physics.
Total wiggle = position uncertainty + (velocity uncertainty × _____).
Using ±50,000 km and ±200 m/s, calculate the uncertainty after six months. Show matching units and the lower and upper x_f bounds.
Describe your graph: label both axes with units, describe the predicted-position line, and explain why the uncertainty band widens.
Choose two of the four traps. Explain how you will avoid each in your own work.
Name the four rubric categories and describe what strong evidence looks like in one of them.
How does the lowest-score rule work? Which part of your work will you improve first, and how?
Write your public paragraph: what we know, what we do not know, why there is uncertainty, and what should happen next. Use numbers, units, and plain language.
